SHA256 values recomputed from the clone on 18 November 2026 and match the crosswalk inventory. The six Algebraic relationships lessons use the older page format with no data-step-id sections; sectionIds are slugs of their numbered card headings.

recommendations: Run a01 to a13 in outline order. Standard 1 students take a01, a03, a04, a05, a07 and a08, then go to math-s12-i01; Standard 2 students take a01 to a07 and a09 to a13 (a08 optional).
Pace flags (gentler Standard pace): a02, a04 and a11 are at risk of rushing; suggested splits are in their packs and entries. a05 should be watched.
Standard 1 coverage: a03 and a04 must show the graph route in every worked example, because Standard 1 does not learn the algebraic methods (a02).
Notation: the syllabus uses y = a^x, y = a^(-x) (a05) and y = k a^x, y = k a^(-x) (a06); the site uses A b^x. Use the syllabus letters on screen.

Seven new site findings are logged as MS-04 to MS-10 in docs/production/claude-pm/site-corrections-maths-standard.md (section 4): two in lesson02, four in lesson03 (MS-06 to MS-09, with MS-08 also covering lesson06 and curriculum-map.json) and one in lesson05.
Kit needs for this strand are in docs/production/claude-pm/checks/maths-standard-kit-needs-a.md; the main new part is a generic coded spreadsheet, which Year 11 Standard also needs many times.

entries.stopBoundary: Build y = k a^x from a story: k is the starting amount (the value at x = 0, the vertical intercept) and a is the multiplier for each step (1 + r for growth by r, 1 − r for decay by r); recognise decay written either as k a^x with 0 < a < 1 or as k a^(−x) with a > 1; use the model to predict with a calculator and round as the context needs; interpret the intercept in words with units. Compound interest and declining-balance depreciation formulas are taught later in the investment strand (math-s12-i02, i03 and i10); this video only uses the general model.

entries.startBoundary: a06's population model predicted 452 000 people in 20 years. Push the same model to 200 years and the answer is absurd. When does a good model stop being good?
entries.stopBoundary: Explain a model's limitations in context: an exponential model assumes the same percentage change every step, grows without any upper limit, and (for decay) never reaches zero; predictions far outside the data (extrapolation) are less reliable than ones inside it; a limitation names the model's assumption and says why that assumption fails in this context. Standard 1 also: a strength of a linear model (simple, constant rate, easy to predict inside the data) and of an exponential model (it captures growth that speeds up, or decay that slows down), and a linear model's limitations (values below zero, rates that change). Graphing a description from words is a08.
entries.recommendation: cid72ff748 is partial: strengths and linear limitations are original teaching. The population simulation (runLogistic, GrowthGraph) can draw a levelling-off curve with lesson labels.

entries.startBoundary: a07 ended on a model that goes flat at a cap. A graph can tell a whole story: going up, staying level, going down. Read a story, then draw it.
entries.stopBoundary: Turn a description into a sketch: choose and label the axes (time usually across), mark the starting value, then for each part of the story decide whether the quantity rises, falls or stays the same, and whether it changes steadily (a straight piece) or speeds up or slows down (a curved piece); steeper means faster; a flat piece means no change; join pieces without gaps when the quantity cannot jump. Match descriptions to graphs. Exact distance-time calculations are math-s12-r12.
entries.recommendation: Standard 1 only (optional for Standard 2). Syllabus-only exception (root ruling 3). Distance-time graphs are math-s12-r12, later; do not rely on them.

entries.startBoundary: Year 11's direct variation: double one quantity and the other doubles (y = kx, a straight line through the origin). Now the opposite: double one and the other halves.
entries.stopBoundary: Recognise inverse variation: x × y stays the same (the constant of variation k), so y = k/x; test a table by multiplying each pair; find k from one pair; graph y = k/x from a table by hand and with an app, avoiding x = 0; the graph is a hyperbola with two separate branches that approach both axes (x = 0 and y = 0) but never meet them; for k > 0 the branches are in the first and third quadrants, for k < 0 in the second and fourth; in practical problems only the first-quadrant branch is used. Building and using models to solve problems, and their limitations, are a13.

entries.stopBoundary: Construct y = k/x for a practical situation: name the two quantities and their units, find k by multiplying one known pair (k is the fixed total, such as a distance or a cost), and write the model; solve for one variable given the other, algebraically (substitute and rearrange, k = xy, x = k/y) or by reading the graph; round in context (round up when a whole number of people, boxes or machines is needed); explain limitations: x = 0 is impossible, very small x gives impossibly large y, fractional answers may be meaningless, and the product may not really stay constant (set-up time, people getting in each other's way).
